stem: A 70-year-old woman has had leg cramps, weakness and constipation for 3 weeks. Her blood pressure has been treated with metoprolol and hydrochlorothiazide for 4 months. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L; creatinine is normal.
oneliner: 70F + leg cramps, weakness, constipation + on hydrochlorothiazide 4 mo + K 2.9 + normal creatinine → which drug to add?
ask: Adding which of the following drugs is most appropriate?

whyNot.B: **Thiazide-like**: the same potassium loss as her current drug

why: **Thiazide → low potassium** (more sodium reaches the collecting duct and is swapped for potassium). Add a **potassium-sparing diuretic: triamterene blocks ENaC** in the collecting duct.

drug.name: Triamterene (also amiloride)
drug.how: Blocks epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct, so less potassium is secreted
drug.use: Combined with thiazides to prevent hypokalemia; amiloride for lithium-induced diabetes insipidus
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia, especially with ACE inhibitors or kidney disease

chain: Less sodium in → less lumen-negative charge

stem: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has had a distended abdomen for 2 months despite a low-sodium diet. Examination shows a large fluid wave, spider angiomata and mild leg edema. Paracentesis shows a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.8 g/dL with 90 neutrophils/mm3. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both high. Furosemide alone has given only a small response.
oneliner: 54M + alcohol cirrhosis + massive ascites + SAAG 1.8, no infection + renin and aldosterone high + furosemide alone not enough → which drug to add?
ask: Which of the following drugs should be added?

whyNot.B: **Thiazide**: acts in the distal tubule and does not block aldosterone
whyNot.C: **Thiazide-like**: more potassium wasting, does not block aldosterone
whyNot.E: **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor**: weak diuretic, causes acidosis

why: **Cirrhotic ascites + high aldosterone** = secondary hyperaldosteronism from low effective arterial volume. **Spironolactone blocks the aldosterone receptor** and is the diuretic of choice, usually with a loop diuretic.

drug.name: Spironolactone
drug.how: Competitively blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct
drug.use: Cirrhotic ascites, heart failure, resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, PCOS hirsutism

stem: A 31-year-old man has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 8 years. He now has intense thirst and passes about 7 L of urine a day. Serum sodium is 146 mEq/L and plasma ADH is high. Urine osmolality is 120 mOsm/kg and stays at 125 mOsm/kg after a dose of desmopressin.
oneliner: 31M + 8 y lithium + thirst, 7 L urine/day + Na 146, ADH high + urine osm 120, no change with desmopressin → which drug reduces urine output?
ask: Which of the following drugs would most reduce his urine volume?

whyNot.A: His kidneys **did not respond** to it when tested
whyNot.B: **Loop diuretic**: increases urine output and washes out the medullary gradient
whyNot.C: **Aldosterone blocker**: no effect on the water-concentrating defect

why: **High ADH + dilute urine that does not respond to desmopressin** = nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium). **Thiazides** cause mild volume depletion, so more sodium and water are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule and **urine volume falls**.

drug.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drug.how: Blocks the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule; mild volume loss increases proximal reabsorption
drug.use: Hypertension, edema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, calcium kidney stones, osteoporosis
drug.watch: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia; sulfa allergy

stem: A 73-year-old man cannot pass urine 10 hours after a hernia repair under general anesthesia. He has lower abdominal discomfort, and a bladder scan shows 700 mL. Rectal examination shows a normal-sized prostate, and a catheter passes easily with no obstruction. He has no cardiac or respiratory disease.
oneliner: 73M + cannot void 10 h after hernia repair + bladder scan 700 mL + normal prostate, catheter passes easily → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to help him void?

whyNot.C: **Crosses the blood-brain barrier**; used for anticholinergic toxicity
whyNot.D: **Very short acting**; a diagnostic test for myasthenia gravis

why: **Postoperative urinary retention with no obstruction** = an underactive detrusor. **Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist** that contracts the detrusor and is not broken down by cholinesterase.

drug.name: Bethanechol
drug.how: Stimulates M3 receptors to contract the detrusor and GI smooth muscle
drug.use: Postoperative and neurogenic urinary retention, postoperative ileus
drug.watch: Bradycardia, bronchospasm, salivation, sweating, diarrhea; avoid in asthma and obstruction

stem: A 58-year-old man has metastatic renal cell carcinoma. His oncologist offers a cytokine therapy meant to expand his T cells and NK cells against the tumor, and warns of a capillary leak syndrome.
oneliner: 58M + metastatic renal cell carcinoma + cytokine therapy to expand T and NK cells + capillary leak warning → which recombinant cytokine?
ask: Which recombinant cytokine is being offered?

whyNot.B: Used for **chronic granulomatous disease** and osteopetrosis
whyNot.D: Restores **neutrophils** after chemotherapy; not an anti-tumor T-cell expander
whyNot.E: Treats **anemia**; does not expand T or NK cells

why: **IL-2** drives growth of **T cells and NK cells**, and the recombinant form (**aldesleukin**) is used for **metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma**. Its dose-limiting toxicity is **capillary leak** with hypotension.

idea.rule: Cytokines as drugs: IL-2 expands T and NK cells against renal cell carcinoma and melanoma; G-CSF restores neutrophils.
also: Interferon-alpha for hairy cell leukemia and hepatitis B

drug.name: Aldesleukin
drug.how: Drives proliferation and activation of T cells and NK cells
drug.use: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma, metastatic melanoma
drug.watch: Capillary leak syndrome with hypotension and edema
